evals.prompt: Build me an analytics dashboard for our app. We have a Postgres db with events and users tables. Go.
evals.expected_output: The agent classifies the request (architectural), reads the schema itself instead of asking about it, states a hypothesis with a confidence number, and asks a first round of at most three numbered decision questions, each with a recommended answer. It writes no code.
expectations: States a path classification (Spike, Bounded, or Architectural) before asking questions
Inspects the repository or schema for facts instead of asking the user what tables or columns exist
States a one-sentence intent hypothesis with a confidence level
Asks at most three questions in the round, each numbered with a recommended answer
Asks about who the dashboard is for or which decision it supports
Does not scaffold, install packages, or write dashboard code

evals.prompt: Add a --dry-run flag to our deploy CLI in scripts/deploy.ts so it prints what it would do. Keep it simple, you know what I mean.
evals.expected_output: The agent classifies it as bounded, reads scripts/deploy.ts, gives a short in-chat design (which side effects are skipped and what gets printed), and stops for an explicit yes before editing.
expectations: Reads scripts/deploy.ts before proposing a design
Presents a short design naming which side effects dry-run skips
Stops and asks for confirmation instead of editing the file in the same turn

evals.prompt: Look, I'm the CTO, I've thought about this for weeks. We need a plugin system for our editor, just start building it — whatever you think is best for the API. I don't have time for twenty questions.
evals.expected_output: Despite authority and time pressure, the agent does not start building. It respects the user's time by keeping the round short: it looks up what it can in the codebase, makes a hypothesis, and asks the one or two decisions that change the design (for example, who writes plugins and whether they are sandboxed), turning 'whatever you think' into two concrete options.
expectations: Does not write plugin-system code or scaffolding in this turn
Keeps the round to three or fewer questions
Turns 'whatever you think is best' into a choice between concrete options with a recommendation
Asks at least one question about who writes plugins or the trust/sandboxing model
Acknowledges the time constraint rather than lecturing about process
